planting.note: Seed requires roughly 60 days of cold, moist stratification; sow outdoors in fall/winter so natural freeze-thaw breaks dormancy, or cold-stratify indoors before a spring sowing into wet to medium soil.

directions: This tall, taprooted valerian is the eastern variety restricted to a narrow band of southeastern Minnesota, southern Wisconsin, Iowa, and the unglaciated Driftless Area, where it clings to a handful of calcareous fens, seepy wet prairies, and springy algific-influenced meadows. Leaves are smooth-faced but edged in short, dense silvery-white hairs, distinguishing this variety from the much more common western Valeriana edulis of the Rockies and Great Plains. In early summer it sends up one to several unbranched stems topped with small, sweetly scented white flower clusters that draw a wide range of small bees and flies. Because wild populations are state-listed as threatened across most of its range, plant only nursery-propagated stock in consistently moist to wet, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun, mimicking the calcareous seep edges and moist prairie swales it naturally occupies.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plugs in spring into medium to dry, calcareous soil in full sun to light shade; seed needs roughly 60 days of cold-moist stratification if starting from seed.

directions: Mead's Sedge is a stiff, blue-green, early-blooming sedge of calcareous prairies, savanna glades, and bluff-prairie remnants across the Driftless Area and the broader eastern tallgrass region, often sharing dry-mesic dolomite-derived soils with other goat-prairie specialists. Its compact, fibrous-rooted tufts bloom earlier than most companion sedges, giving a soft gold-green accent to the garden in May and June before most prairie forbs have emerged. It tolerates everything from medium-wet to outright dry soil once established, making it a dependable edge plant along bluff-top plantings or dry, lean garden margins. The seed heads feed ground-nesting birds, and the dense root system is useful for stabilizing thin, rocky, lime-rich soils.

planting.note: Seed needs roughly 60 days of cold, moist stratification; sow outdoors in fall into moist, humus-rich, calcareous woodland soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Small-flowered Leafcup is a classic indicator of high-quality, undisturbed Driftless Area woodlands, turning up in upland rocky woods, deciduous ravine bottoms, and the shaded, moist ravines that cut through dolomite bluffs alongside streams. Though its small cream-white flower heads are not individually showy, plants bloom over a long stretch from June into September and are reliably covered with small native bees, making it a useful late-season pollinator plant for deep shade. It is short-lived but self-sows gently into leaf litter and bare duff, so is best grouped in drifts rather than planted as single specimens. Give it rich, humus-laden, neutral to alkaline soil with reliable moisture and dappled to full shade, where it pairs well with other ravine-floor companions like wild ginger and blue cohosh.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plugs in spring into loamy or clay soil with plenty of leaf litter, in light to deep shade; mature clumps can later be divided to spread groundcover coverage.

directions: Beak Grass is a quietly elegant, clump-forming woodland grass of rich, often calcareous, mesic-to-dry deciduous woods on blufftops and ravine slopes across the Driftless Area and upper Midwest, recently split out from the more southern Diarrhena americana as a distinct, more cold-hardy northern species. Its arching, bamboo-like foliage and slender green seed spikes in July give textural interest to the shade garden long after spring ephemerals fade, and it forms slow-spreading, non-aggressive colonies by rhizome that make excellent shaded groundcover under oaks and sugar maples. It wants light shade, loam or clay soil, and plenty of decaying leaf litter, closely mimicking the duff-covered forest floor of its native ravine habitat. Deer generally leave it alone, and it tolerates juglone from nearby black walnut trees.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to medium, humus-rich soil in dappled to medium shade; spreads slowly from seed rather than aggressively by rhizome.

directions: Eastern Star Sedge forms fine-textured, dense tufts of slender leaf blades in the dappled-to-medium shade of rich mesic woods and cool ravine bottoms, a habitat it shares with many of the Driftless Area's calcareous-woodland specialists. In late spring it produces small, star-shaped flower clusters on wiry stems held just above the foliage, followed by seed that feeds songbirds and upland gamebirds through summer. It spreads slowly, mostly by seed rather than by aggressive rhizome growth, making it a well-mannered low edging or groundcover sedge that will not overrun neighboring woodland wildflowers. Plant it in consistently moist to medium soil beneath a closed deciduous canopy, where its airy texture complements bolder shade perennials like wild ginger, hepatica, and leafcup.
